tip: The fastest way to ask a price. Point at the item while you say it — no full sentence needed.
Point at the menu item while you say it. Works in restaurants, markets and shops alike.
Say it when you order. In Sichuan and Hunan restaurants they may ask 要辣吗? ("Spicy?") first.
The 吗 at the end turns a statement into a question — the simplest question form in Chinese.
Literally "good to eat". Saying it during the meal is a genuine compliment in China.
Handy because 肉 covers pork, beef and lamb — you don't need to name each animal.
Chinese restaurants usually bring hot water or tea by default. Ask for 冰水 (bīng shuǐ) if you want ice water.

english: Can I get this to go?
tip: 打包 literally means "hit-pack". Doggy bags are normal and free in most Chinese restaurants.
Say it with a smile — in markets this often starts friendly bargaining rather than ending it.
Literally "buy the bill". This is the standard way to ask to pay in mainland China; in Taiwan people say 结账 (jiézhàng).
公共厕所 (gōnggòng cèsuǒ, public restroom) is common on Chinese streets and usually free.

english: I need to go to the airport.
tip: Show it to a taxi driver together with your flight details.
Hand your phone over and say this to confirm it is the right place. Chinese addresses are hard to read aloud, so always show the written address as well.
张 is a measure word. Chinese needs one between a number and its noun.
哪儿 is the casual spoken version of 哪里 — you will hear both constantly.
Say this first and people often switch to simpler words or start helping with gestures.
一下 softens a request — it makes asking for help sound polite rather than demanding.

english: I want to buy a ticket.
tip: Works at train stations, bus terminals, cinemas and tourist attractions.
Ask this at bus and train stations where departure times aren't posted in English.
的 links the owner to the thing — the same pattern builds "my bag", "my ticket" and "my hotel".
了 shows the booking already happened. Say it at check-in with your confirmation ready.

english: Do you have a room available?
tip: A walk-in phrase. 满 (mǎn, full) is the answer you don't want — if they say 满了, try the next hotel.
Have your passport ready — hotels in China must register every guest, including foreigners.
退房 literally means "return the room". Hand back the key card while you say it.

english: What floor is the room on?
tip: Chinese lifts often label floors as 1F, 2F. Note that 一楼 is the ground floor, not the first floor up.
"Wi-Fi" is pronounced almost the same in Chinese. Staff will usually point at the password.
Swap in any noun and the pattern holds — 灯坏了 (the light), 马桶坏了 (the toilet).
Chinese hotels normally provide bath towels but not washcloths — ask housekeeping if you want one.
Most hotels hold bags for free after check-out — very handy on your last travel day.
几点 is how you ask "what time" for any event — just swap in the activity.
Add 这个 while pointing — much clearer than asking about nothing in a crowded stall.
The standard opening move in markets. Expect to settle somewhere near the middle.
Repeating a verb (试试) means "have a little try" — softer and friendlier than the single form.
This is the polite way to decline a shop assistant who follows you around the store.
Swap 颜色 (color) for 尺码 (chǐmǎ, size) to ask for a different size with the same sentence.
Alipay and WeChat Pay dominate daily payments in China. Small shops may be cash-only.

english: Do you have a small size?
tip: Sizes are 小号 small, 中号 medium, 大号 large. Chinese sizes usually run smaller than US sizes.
Bags are usually free at supermarkets but often charged a few cents at convenience stores.
Keep your receipt (发票 fāpiào). Returns without one are rare in Chinese shops.
打折 means to give a discount. Big malls have fixed prices — ask this in markets, small shops and tourist streets, where a polite ask often works.
Literally "you good". A safe, universal greeting at any hour of the day.
Say it as one doubled word: xièxie. Add 你 to thank one person directly (谢谢你), or 大家 to thank a whole group (谢谢大家).
Covers both a real apology and getting someone's attention in a crowd.
The standard reply to 谢谢. 客气 literally means "to stand on ceremony", so 不客气 is "don't be so polite".
Literally "see you again". Among friends you will also hear 拜拜 (báibái), borrowed from "bye-bye".
Textbook Chinese. Between native speakers you will hear 最近怎么样 or a remark about something visible; 你好吗 turns up mostly in teaching material and in what people say to foreign learners.
Answer with 我叫… (wǒ jiào…) plus your name. To give your surname politely, say 我姓… (wǒ xìng…).
Short and clear. Pair it with 请再说一遍 and most people will slow down for you.
遍 is the measure word for an action done once, from beginning to end.
The most useful two-syllable phrase in China: it gets attention, makes a light apology, and softens a refusal. Use it before a question or when you squeeze past someone.

words.en: to feel embarrassed / to have the nerve

tip: 推荐 means to recommend. Ask it and the server will usually point at one or two dishes — the fastest way to eat well without reading a long menu.
素 means vegetarian. In a noisy restaurant 素 is easy to miss, so add 不要肉 ("no meat") if you want to be certain.
Rice refills are usually free. 加 means to add, so the same pattern gives you 加汤 (more soup) or 加水 (more water).
Unlike 不要辣 (said when ordering), this one is for food that is already on the table. 太…了 is the "too much" frame — 太贵了 works the same way.

pinyin: Qǐng dài wǒ qù zhège dìzhǐ.
english: Please take me to this address.
tip: The sentence that makes taxis easy: show the address on your phone and read it out. 带 means to take someone somewhere.

english: How long does it take to get there?
tip: Ask before you get in, not after. 多久 asks about a length of time; 几点 asks what time (on the clock).

pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī méi diàn le.
tip: 没电 literally means "no electricity". Useful when you need to show a map, charge your phone or pay — nearly every payment in China runs through a phone.

pinyin: Kěyǐ bāng wǒ pāi zhāng zhàopiàn ma?
english: Can you take a photo of me?
tip: Hand your phone over first, then ask. 张 is the measure word for photos — 拍张照片 is "take a photo", 拍照 is the general verb.

english: Do you have a larger size?
tip: 大号 = large, 中号 = medium, 小号 = small. Swap 大 for 小 and you already have the other question.

english: Can I get a tax refund?
tip: Only shops with a 退税 sign can do this, and you need to spend at least 500 yuan in one store on one day. Bring your passport — the refund happens at the airport.
In China the question is usually the other way round — many places prefer 微信 or 支付宝. Ask before you queue, and keep some cash for small stalls and taxis.
Chinese rarely answers with a bare yes — it repeats the verb instead: 是 (it is), 有 (I have), 可以 (sure). 对 (duì) means "correct" and is what you'll hear most.
不是 negates 是 only. For "I don't have it" say 没有 (méiyǒu), and for a flat refusal 不用了，谢谢.
Drop 请问 in front of any question and it instantly sounds polite — literally "please may I ask". Every local does this in shops and station queues.
Before roughly 10 a.m. 你好 works at any hour, but 早上好 sounds warmer in the morning — shopkeepers and hotel staff notice the difference.
Only for going to sleep or leaving late. When you arrive somewhere at night, the greeting is 晚上好 (wǎnshang hǎo) — a different phrase.
好 alone works too, but 好的 sounds friendlier and softer — the one to use with staff, drivers and hosts.
Different from 我不懂 ("I don't understand"). This one means "I have no idea" — say it and people will usually point you to someone else.

pinyin: Wǒ Zhōngwén shuō de bù hǎo.
tip: Say it early and people switch to simpler Chinese or write things down instead of giving up on you mid-sentence.
会 is about a learned skill. Swap it for 能 and the question shifts from "do you speak English?" to "could you say it in English?".
一点 means "a little" and softens the request — a bare 说慢 sounds like an order. Same pattern: 便宜一点 (a bit cheaper).
The most useful sentence when you are stuck. People write faster than they can explain, and characters you can copy are characters you can look up.
For partners and family. Between friends Chinese says 我很喜欢你 ("I really like you") — 爱 is strong and saying it casually can land oddly.
Literally "dry the glass". Say it as the glasses meet — and in China you are expected to actually drink when someone toasts you, so pour accordingly.
快乐 is the "happy" in every greeting: swap the front and you get 新年快乐 (Happy New Year) and 节日快乐 (Happy holidays).
The standard reply to 对不起 (sorry) — and what you say when someone apologises for bumping into you. Not to be confused with 不客气, which replies to thank you.
一下 softens a request the way "just" does in English — 等 alone sounds abrupt, 等一下 is what you'll hear all day in China.
The polite way to turn down touts, taxi drivers and street sellers. 不用 literally means "no need" — firmer than it sounds, and it ends the conversation cleanly.
Literally "knowing you is very happy". On business cards and at formal meetings you'll also see the short version 幸会 (xìnghuì).
Said early, it buys patience — it explains your accent before anyone has to guess, and people slow down for you.
太…了 is the "so / too …" frame. 棒 means excellent — the same frame with a different adjective gives you 太好了 (that's great) and 太辣了 (too spicy).
Only for real danger — 救命 literally means "save my life". For a small favour use 我需要帮助 instead.
Calmer and more general than 救命. 需要 is "to need" — reuse the frame as 我需要看医生 or 我需要一张地图.
China's emergency numbers: 110 police, 120 ambulance, 119 fire. All three are free from any phone, including a locked one.
救护车 is the ambulance and 120 is its number. If words fail completely, saying "one-two-zero" out loud is understood everywhere.
迷路 means to lose your way. Show the Chinese name of your hotel on your phone while you say it — names are far more reliable than directions.
The same 在哪里 pattern as 厕所在哪里. Swap in 药店 (pharmacy) or 派出所 (local police station) and you are covered.

english: I need to see a doctor.
tip: In China you usually go straight to a hospital's 急诊 (emergency department) rather than booking an appointment with a clinic.
Add the thing with 对…过敏: 我对花生过敏. Say it before you order, and show it written down — in a busy kitchen it is easy to lose.
Swap 花生 for 海鲜 (seafood), 牛奶 (milk) or 坚果 (nuts). Watch for 花生油 (peanut oil) too — it is common in Chinese cooking.
了 marks the change — you were fine before and you are not now. If it is a fever, 我发烧 (wǒ fāshāo) is more specific and gets you seen faster.
File a police report (报警) before you contact your embassy — the replacement needs that paper, and it is also what your insurance will ask for.

pinyin: Wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le.
tip: 被 marks the passive voice — literally "my wallet was stolen". If you simply lost it, use 丢了 instead: 我的钱包丢了.
Chinese pharmacies are 药店 and are marked with a green cross. 附近 means "nearby" and slots in front of any place you need.
支付宝 (Zhīfùbǎo) and 微信支付 are how China pays for almost everything, from taxis to noodle shops. Ask before you order, and have the app open with your card already added.

english: Can I pay with WeChat Pay?
tip: 微信支付 (Wēixìn zhīfù) is the other half of the pair. Both apps look the same at the till: you show a payment code (付款码) and the cashier scans it.
The all-purpose question when you cannot see a card reader. In most shops the answer is 扫码 (sǎo mǎ) — scan the QR code.
来 here means "let me do it". Say it as you reach for the QR code — it settles who pays without a discussion.
请客 means to host someone as a guest. In China splitting the bill is less common than one person covering it, and saying this first is how you claim it.
Use it at the till when you have several items, or at the end of a meal. 一共 means "in total".
分开 means separately. Useful when you are travelling in a group and want one bill split — say it before the cashier starts scanning.
Literally "no need to give change". 找钱 is the verb for handing change back, so 找 alone is understood here.
发票 (fāpiào) is the official tax receipt, not a printed till slip — you need it for expense claims and for tax refunds at the airport. Ask before you pay if you can.
Say it and show your screen — 没 means "did not". If the money left your account anyway, ask for 退款 (tuìkuǎn, a refund).

pinyin: Wǒ de kǎ bù néng yòng.
tip: Foreign cards often fail on Chinese payment terminals, so the usual fix is Alipay or WeChat Pay instead. 不能用 is a useful frame on its own: 这个不能用 (this one doesn't work).
Sturdier than 不要辣 for seafood — cooks hear 不吃 as a hard rule. Sauces can still hide shrimp stock, so pair it with 我过敏 if your reaction is severe.
Metro systems in Chinese cities are cheap, fast and signed in English — this sentence saves the walk. Staff will often draw you a mini-map when you ask.
The sentence taxi and Didi drivers hear a hundred times a day. Say it while pointing at the curb; use it a street early if traffic makes pulling over difficult.
Works for museums, shops and scenic areas alike — swap 关门 for 开门 and it asks about opening. Many smaller sights stop selling tickets an hour before closing, so ask before you queue.
Some museums and temples ban flash or all photography, and staff will stop you mid-shot. Asking first earns a smile even when the answer is a headshake.
Front desks usually hand over a card with the password, but asking directly is faster than waiting to be understood. Codes mix capitals and digits, so 请写下来 helps here too.
Standard checkout in China is noon, and many hotels grant an extra hour or two for free if you ask in the morning. Need the whole afternoon? That becomes a half-day-rate conversation.
The one-sentence fix for street-facing rooms, thin walls and late-night karaoke. Hotels would rather move you than argue — ask the same evening, not the next morning.
Banks and airport counters exchange cash, but mobile pay has made counters rare in most cities — ask at your hotel first. Often the better rate is simply withdrawing yuan at a bank ATM.
Use it at licensed exchange desks and check the answer against your banking app — a rate noticeably worse than the app's is the signal to walk out. Cash exchange needs your passport.

The escape hatch when a menu has no photos and no English: hand the choice to the staff and let them pick local favorites within your budget. Say an ingredient you cannot eat first (我不吃海鲜) so the pick is safe.

Hot water is everywhere in China and usually free — restaurants bring a kettle to the table, and hotel desks fill your bottle without blinking. It is also the polite way to decline cold drinks if your stomach is sensitive.

The partner phrase to 不要辣 — Chinese home-style cooking seasons generously, and salt is the other adjustment kitchens actually make. Say it while ordering, not when the dish arrives; after-cooking fixes are much rarer.
For hair-raising rides when you cannot read the meter debate fast enough. Drivers take it seriously — 开 names the driving, and 一点 softens it into a request instead of an accusation.

english: Please tell me when we arrive.
tip: Lets you doze or read on any bus or shared ride without missing your stop. It also covers the night-train berth and the long-distance cab — drivers almost always honor it because it costs them nothing.

english: Can I get a wake-up call tomorrow morning?
tip: Front desks still run wake-up calls in China and take them more reliably than a foreign phone's alarm plus jet lag. Say it with the time — 明早七点 (tomorrow 7 a.m.) — and the desk logs it for you.
Budget hotels often keep hairdryers at the front desk instead of in the room, so this question beats silently searching the closet. Same pattern works for adapters: 有转换器吗？

english: This one is a bit big.
tip: The fitting-room sentence that keeps the sale moving: say 有点大 and the seller brings a smaller size without you hunting shelves. 有点 is deliberately soft — it signals 'adjust this', not 'I hate it'.

You will need it more than you expect: last entry times, last metro trains, and store closings all run earlier in China than the sign suggests. The answer is a number plus 点 — 五点 (five o'clock) — so you will even understand it.

english: I need to contact my embassy.
tip: The formal phrase for lost passports and worse — hotel staff and police recognize 大使馆 instantly and will usually help you call. Say your country's Chinese name after it if you can (美国 America, 英国 Britain, 澳大利亚 Australia).

Cilantro lands on everything in China — soups, noodles, cold dishes, even some drinks. Servers often ask 加不加香菜 ("add cilantro or not?"), so this is an everyday reflex. Same pattern: 不要葱 (bú yào cōng) for no scallions.
一份 is the measure word for one serving or one dish. Point at the dish while you say it. For drinks swap the measure word: 再来一杯 (yì bēi, one more cup), 再来一瓶 (yì píng, one more bottle).
离 marks distance between two places — 这里离市中心 = "here to downtown". The natural follow-up is 多远 (duō yuǎn, how far). Handy for judging taxi rides, hotel locations and walking routes.

pinyin: Zhè tàng chē qù jīchǎng ma?
english: Does this train go to the airport?
tip: 趟 is the measure word for a trip, so 这趟车 means "this run of the bus/train". Swap the destination freely: 去火车站吗 (the train station?), 去市中心吗 (downtown?). Works for metro lines, buses and airport shuttles.

pinyin: Kěyǐ bāng wǒ jiào chūzūchē ma?
english: Can you call a taxi for me?
tip: Front desks call taxis for guests as a matter of course — or hail one on an app (滴滴 Didi) for you. Note the difference: 出租车 is a metered street cab, 网约车 (wǎngyuēchē) is an app-hailed car.

Happens constantly — key cards demagnetize next to phones, or lose power right after checkout time. Take the card (not just the problem) to the front desk; they recharge it in seconds, no re-check-in needed.
取钱 means withdraw; 存钱 (cún qián) means deposit. Foreign cards work at big-bank ATMs — 中国银行 (Bank of China), 工商银行 (ICBC), 建设银行 (CCB) — and most machines offer an English menu.
The happy twin of 我不懂 (I don't understand). Say it with a nod when directions finally click. 明白 also works alone as a short "Got it" — very common in conversation.
肚子 is the belly, 疼 means hurts. Swap the body part and the pattern still works: 头疼 (tóu téng, headache), 喉咙疼 (hóulóng téng, sore throat). Pharmacists and doctors understand this instantly.

First stop at an airport is the 行李查询 (luggage inquiry) desk with your baggage tag. 丢 covers lost, misplaced and stolen — it starts the search without accusing anyone. Airlines in China handle this routinely.
Mostly useful near borders and in tourist hotels — the honest answer in most of China is no. 美金 is the spoken word for US dollars; 美元 (měiyuán) is the written one, and both are understood.

The question to ask before any money move — changing cash, a foreign-card ATM withdrawal or a wire at the bank. 手续费 is the universal word for a service fee, and it is sometimes negotiable at exchange counters.
Worth asking for bulky souvenirs — teapots, art, furniture. Big shops may offer international shipping or help with a forwarder; small stalls will not. 寄 covers mail and parcel shipping in one word.

pinyin: Mǎi liǎng jiàn kěyǐ piányi ma?
english: Any discount if I buy two?
tip: The bulk-discount line, and sellers almost always move for a second item — 件 is the measure word for clothes. Same frame works with any number: 买三件 (buy three). Pairs with 可以便宜一点吗.

english: I want to refund this ticket.
tip: Say it at the original ticket window with the ticket and your passport. Train tickets refund for a fee by departure time and the rules tighten close to the train — so go as soon as plans change.
过 here means "went past" — the sentence is the polite way to ask for help without panic. On the metro the fix is easy: stay on to the next stop and ride back. On a bus, tell the driver 再停一下.

english: What time is the next one?
tip: 班 is the measure word for scheduled runs — buses, ferries, metro trains. If the answer stumps you, the follow-up is 多久一班 (duō jiǔ yì bān, how often does one come).

english: I'd like to stay one more night.
tip: 续住 means extend the stay — ask the night before, because rooms booked through apps are often released for resale on the morning of checkout. Swap 一晚 for 两晚 (two nights) freely.
The agreement word for everything: a request, a change of plan, a thank-you. Literally "no problem exists". Pair it with 没关系 (it's fine) — one says yes, the other forgives.

english: I got separated from my friend.
tip: The standard sentence at information desks, station staff and police — they deal with it daily. Have a meeting spot in mind before big crowds; phones die and signals drop in the metro, which is exactly when this happens.
微 means slightly — 微辣 is the lowest heat level on most menus, between 不辣 (no spice) and 中辣 (medium). Point at the 辣度 on the menu while saying this and you cannot be misunderstood.
Works for restaurant lines, ticket queues and food pickup alike. The answer is usually a number plus 分钟 (fēnzhōng, minutes) — for example 二十分钟 (twenty minutes).
线 is the word for metro lines — Line 2 is simply 2号线. Staff usually answer with the direction too, like 往浦东 (bound for Pudong), so listen for 往 or 开往 (bound for).

english: Is there a convenience store nearby?
tip: Chains like 便利蜂, 罗森 (Lawson) and 全家 (FamilyMart) sell water, chargers and snacks, most open around the clock. Swap the last word: 药店 (yàodiàn) pharmacy, 超市 (chāoshì) supermarket.
Say it at the front desk or hang the make-up-room door tag — housekeeping in Chinese hotels usually runs 9am to 2pm. 一下 softens the request into something polite and brief.
Chinese taps are labelled 热水 (hot) and 冷水 (cold). If the shower truly has no hot water, report it at the desk — pairs with 空调坏了 for reporting room problems.
Ask before you pay — many Chinese hotel rates are 不退不改 (no refund, no change). 免费取消 is the exact phrase booking sites use for free cancellation, so you will see it everywhere.

english: Can you deliver it to my hotel?
tip: Common for bulky buys like luggage or tea sets — shops use 同城快递 (same-city courier), arriving same or next day. Have the hotel's Chinese address ready on your phone.
For cuts, sprains and falls. Add the body part: 腿 (tuǐ) leg, 手 (shǒu) hand, 头 (tóu) head. For serious bleeding call 120 for an ambulance — see 请叫救护车.

english: Can you turn on the AC?
tip: Standard in taxis and DiDi rides in summer — drivers sometimes leave it off to save fuel. 开 means on; if you are cold, say 请关空调 (please turn it off) or 请调低一点 (please turn it down).
